label: Two Faces of Ricci Curvature
notes: This chapter opens Part III by contrasting two readings of lower Ricci bounds. The analytic reading lives on smooth manifolds and computes a tensor in coordinates. The synthetic reading lives on any metric-measure space and tests convexity of entropy. The whole part shows the two agree where both apply.

label: The Analytic Definition
notes: Analytically the Ricci tensor is built from the Levi-Civita connection by contracting the Riemann curvature. A lower bound asks that this symmetric tensor dominate K times the metric at every point. The definition is local, coordinate-dependent, and demands the metric be at least twice differentiable to even write down.

label: What the Analytic View Buys
notes: Because the Ricci tensor is a pointwise object it is checkable by differentiation and feeds directly into Bochner formulas, comparison theorems, and volume bounds. These are the classical tools of Riemannian geometry. The cost is rigidity: the formula presupposes smoothness and says nothing about singular or limiting spaces.

label: Where Smoothness Fails
notes: Sequences of manifolds with a fixed Ricci bound can converge in Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a limit that is no longer a manifold. Cones, collapsed spaces, and weighted spaces appear. The analytic tensor cannot be evaluated on such a limit, so a bound expressed only through derivatives simply does not survive the passage.

label: Metric-Measure Spaces
notes: The synthetic stage is a metric-measure space: a complete separable metric space carrying a reference measure. No charts, no tensor, no differentiability are assumed. The Wasserstein space of probability measures over this base becomes the arena where curvature is reformulated through the geometry of optimal transport.

label: Entropy on Wasserstein Space
notes: The Boltzmann entropy functional, the integral of the density times its logarithm against the reference measure, is the central observable. Its behaviour along Wasserstein geodesics encodes curvature. Where the measure has no density relative to the reference, the entropy is set to plus infinity, which already filters admissible interpolations.

label: Displacement Convexity Is the Bound
notes: The synthetic definition declares a lower Ricci bound K by requiring the entropy to be K-convex along every Wasserstein geodesic. Convexity of one functional replaces positivity of a tensor. The inequality involves only distances and measures, so it makes sense verbatim on any metric-measure space.

label: The Two Views Agree
notes: On a smooth weighted manifold the Bochner identity converts the Hessian of entropy along transport into a Ricci integral. So K-displacement convexity of entropy holds exactly when the Ricci tensor dominates K times the metric. The synthetic test reproduces the analytic one with no loss, anchoring the new definition.

label: Stability Under Limits
notes: The synthetic inequality is phrased in distances and entropies, quantities that pass to Gromov-Hausdorff and measured limits. So a lower bound that holds along a sequence holds in the limit. This is the decisive advantage: the curvature condition is closed, exactly the property the analytic tensor lacked.

label: Analytic Hessian vs Synthetic Chords
notes: The notebook's lab makes the contrast tactile. A finite-difference Hessian of a convex profile becomes unstable at a kink, while the chord inequality, comparing a midpoint value to the average of endpoints, stays valid. Checkability and stability are different virtues; the synthetic chord test keeps the second one.

label: Alexandrov and the Lineage
notes: The move from tensors to chord inequalities echoes Alexandrov geometry, where sectional curvature bounds are encoded by triangle comparison rather than by a curvature tensor. Lott, Villani, Sturm carry the same philosophy to Ricci bounds via entropy convexity, giving the CD spaces studied through the rest of the part.

label: The Program of Part III
notes: Part III builds the synthetic theory: define curvature-dimension conditions, prove they are stable and consistent with the smooth case, and recover functional and geometric inequalities. This chapter is the manifesto. Keep both readings side by side, demanding that any definition be both checkable on smooth spaces and stable under limits.
